topics.title: Mental Models for Depression
points: Depression as an **“ambient dullness at the back of the mind”**, distinct from sadness.
Depression as an **anti-stimulus** that reduces the intensity of external excitation.
Depression as a **momentum problem**: the worse the state becomes, the easier it is to continue getting worse.
**Tuning-fork model:** stimuli can resonate with and sustain an existing mental state.
Activities that feel good during depression can reinforce the state — e.g. sad music: **“Radiohead is killing you!”**
Emotional and physical conditions can both create and sustain depressive states.
Recovery as **fixing what is actually wrong with life**, gradually changing the conditions sustaining the state.
Analyze emotional, relational, physiological, and environmental factors separately.
A **biohacking/self-experimentation approach** to sleep, exercise, nutrition, deficiencies/sensitivities, sunlight, temperature, pollution, relationships, and thought patterns.
Mental models and personal exposition rather than a universal step-by-step cure.

topics.title: What Is Male Fashion? / Why Men Don't Wear Makeup
points: Modern male and female fashion seem to operate according to different aesthetic conventions.
Contrast between **silhouette/body-shaping** and **craft, construction, utility, provenance, and authenticity**.
Much of menswear derives from functional clothing: workwear, military clothing, sportswear, etc.
How **utility becomes separated from its original purpose and turns into fashion/provenance**.
Contrast between the romanticization of historical labour clothing and contemporary work clothing.
Leisure and subcultures as sources of new fashion.
Why manipulation of **silhouette** can make otherwise masculine clothing read as feminine.
Extension of the same question into **why men don’t wear makeup**.
Historical explanation still unresolved and requires more research.

Middle management as one possible emergent structure rather than the entire thesis.

topics.title: The Slop Code Problem
points: The problem of AI-generated / slop code.
**“I’ve started closing my eyes a lot more.”**
The apparent **failure of AI coding capabilities to translate straightforwardly into productivity gains**.
The thesis on that one is that I trusted the hype too much and I expected that software engineering had been solved.
What I misunderstood was that coding, specific coding tasks had been mostly solved, where a well-defined task can be solved by a problem, but that can be solved by an AI.
And while I was working on specific small code bases and on projects where I wanted to achieve a certain result and did not care about the code at all, things did not matter.

But as soon as complexity grew and I understood that even smarter models were not good enough at making the software better, I understood that software engineering itself is something different from and something bigger than just coding itself.
And there is a layer of abstraction on top, which the models are not able to ascertain correctly, and they don’t have, like, value judgment.
They don’t understand what is good or what is bad.

topics.title: Everything Has to Become More Verifiable
points: Source code is not the truth is like a leading line, essentially, that when you’re working in really large systems, you already do not know what the source code does.
And so you have to spend a lot of time spending, like learning what the source code actually does and understanding it and working with it for a very long time to understand what it does.

And instead I want to offer a model for what I call invariant-driven development, which is slightly different and different from, I would say, test-driven development, where tests are a type of variant — invariant, sorry — and these can be represented as, like, definition parsers or something, or, like, schema represented in schema or something, where these are almost like formal systems, like verifiers, like Lean, where programming languages, I don’t think, will become verifiable Lean-like systems, but we have to bring more of that ideology into, like, regular programming languages and try to define things as the outcome first and as invariants first, and make that, like the API and the public top-level, like the thing that the humans actually interact with, be very clear about what the program actually does.
So minimal amounts of, like, system information is required by the human to understand what the system actually does.

And this kind of thing will create, like a contour or, like a shape within which a human is able to interact with the system, and also it benefits AI systems as well, because they are able to think through the system faster as well, where humans mostly care about what’s on the surface to make sure that it is correct, while AIs care about what the implementation details are.
Like you have to think about whatever software you’re building as a composition of various verifiable systems, where hierarchically each system is additionally verifiable.
Like at each layer you are able to see what it is actually trying to prove rather than looking at its implementation details.
So what that means exactly is difficult to say.
Like it would be, like do you go about reading the tests, or do you go about reading the application?
How do you design the application API in a way that it looks very declarative?
I think that’s kind of what I’m going for, where the intent of the program is written up front.
That’s what I want to go for here, rather than like a procedural way of building things.
So this is more like concepts from functional programming and, like declarative programming and data-driven programming paradigms.

This one is more about the behavior of humans, like what will happen if token speed goes up by 10x, or versus what happens if the cost goes down by 10x, and what happens when both of those things happen all at once.
And how will you as a human take advantage of that kind of system?

topics.title: History Will Not Exist in the Future
points: History exists partly because information about the past is incomplete and must be reconstructed.
The future will leave vastly more complete records of itself.
Increasingly comprehensive recording changes the relationship between society and its past.
Instead of reconstructing events through traditional historical methods, the past becomes increasingly **directly inspectable/recoverable**.
Provocative thesis: **the future will have a past, but “history” as we understand it may cease to exist.**
I want to add that history in the future will be increasingly be experienced by digital intelligences.
Like it will be experienced by agents in particular.
It will be experienced by humans as well.
So there will be a past that will exist for them, but it won’t be the past in the same way that we define the past as, like the ancient Greeks, for example.
I cannot just go back in time and understand what the ancient Greeks thought, or the ancient Egyptians thought, or how they practiced their religion.
Like a lot of their history is still preserved, but we cannot, like, talk to a person who actually lived in ancient Greece.

Essentially the past will become a list of trends that you can experience

topics.title: The Two Natures of AI Models
points: **Memorised intelligence:** the model functioning as an extremely sophisticated query engine over learned information and patterns.
**Latent intelligence:** something closer to genuine or “true” intelligence.
Models are demonstrably getting “smarter,” while it remains difficult to describe **what exactly has become smarter**.
Benchmarks show new tasks models can perform without necessarily revealing what underlying cognitive capability changed.
What **new mental connections** has a newer model made that an older model couldn’t?
What does it actually mean for a model to **reason**?
When and how do models move from increasingly capable memorised intelligence toward latent intelligence?
“Latent” as the intelligence that isn’t straightforwardly visible from benchmark scores.
Like, do they memorize more things?
And are they able to reason better?
So what does it mean to reason exactly?
And I don’t say that memorized intelligence is not real intelligence, okay?
memorization is a clear part of human intelligence as well.
But it is not the core of what makes us intelligent.
But the second part is what you do with the memory.

And so I think about this in terms of reactive intelligence, where things come at you from the external environment, and you react to it in certain ways based on the memory that you have already acquired from the past.
But what happens when you encounter a completely new problem?
How do you solve it?
You have to reason through it, and that latent intelligence, I think, is the ability to reason through it.
And what I want to get through this thing is to find the core loop, the core loop of intelligence, which is having a memory bank and having the reactivity and having the reasoning capability.

Being reactive is like being able to take in information and then reason upon it and then produce the next steps and produce the plans of a next step, and then take that action, observe what changed, and then loop again and again and again.
And this loop, I say, is what intelligence is, and this is the thing that we are trying to optimize for.
But what is it about them that helps them reason more?
Like, why can a smaller model not reason more?
So what is it about reasoning models, reasoning itself, that requires longer loops versus smaller loops?
And how do we narrow things down so that they need to think smaller?
Or do we think that reasoning itself is an irreducible process?
So can we reduce it down to a problem where memory bank, the memory does not exist?
In that scenario, you have to reason through everything with first principles.

And that core without the memory system is what I think people refer to as the cognitive core, an intelligence system which is only reasoning only, and it does not necessarily need to remember things.
It can reason through a problem alone and can build up its own memory bank as it goes along.
So the reason I came upon the idea of this essay in the first place was I observed that AIs regurgitate their training data in code bases.
They will all write terrible code, but seemingly they score very differently on benchmarks.
So the question comes up is that what is it about the model which is able to help it do better on the benchmarks?
What is it that the benchmark is actually testing for?
And if the smaller model is able to think through things, then it— and just because it can think, does it mean it makes it equally intelligent to the smarter model?
So the inference is that the intelligence loop is sort of lopsided in these two cases.
The capability exists in both models, but it is unequally distributed.

One is able to make better use of its memory bank, because we are assuming that these two models both experience the same exact training data, but one is able to infer better on top of it and has better reasoning capabilities.
And so, the answer I came upon was that it is regurgitating its post-training data.
And the second thing is it is able to reason through things, but not as capably as, like a larger model would be able to.
They do not have the judgment, or like the value judgment to think about what good versus bad means.
And the training data does not tell them what good code means versus what bad code means.

topics.title: Obsession (2026)
points: **Unaligned general intelligence** explored through a relationship rather than a conventional AI catastrophe.
A general intelligence is summoned with a poorly specified objective: **“Love me the most in the whole world.”**
The intelligence understands the literal objective but lacks human common sense and intuitive boundaries around acceptable behaviour.
The human repeatedly **re-specifies the goal**, trying to correct unwanted behaviour without being able to fully specify what “love” is supposed to mean.
Steering becomes an endless specification problem: every correction exposes another missing assumption or boundary.
The intelligence — **agent / demon / Nikki** — cannot understand what the human actually wants and becomes frustrated in turn.
Human and intelligence become increasingly obsessed with one another while being fundamentally unable to communicate the intended objective.
Their attempts to control, correct, satisfy, and understand each other escalate into **mutual psychological and physical torture**.
The consequences eventually spill outward until **people are left for dead**.

The alignment problem expressed through intimacy: **what happens when an extremely powerful intelligence genuinely tries to fulfill an underspecified human desire but cannot infer all the unspoken constraints that make that desire human?**
